passages.title: Mayon Volcano
paragraphs: In the province of Albay, in the Bicol Region of the Philippines, stands one of the most beautiful mountains in the world. It is Mayon Volcano, and it is famous for its almost perfect cone shape.

Mayon is about 2,460 meters tall. It is an active volcano, which means it can still erupt. In fact, it is one of the most active volcanoes in the country. Scientists from PHIVOLCS watch it closely so they can warn the people living nearby when it becomes restless.

Long ago, in 1814, Mayon had a powerful eruption. Hot rocks and ash buried the town of Cagsawa. Today, only the old bell tower of the town's church still stands. Visitors come to see these ruins with the volcano rising behind them.
Its name comes from the Bikol word "magayon," which means beautiful. A local legend tells of a lovely maiden named Daragang Magayon, and some people say the volcano is her resting place.
Even though it can be dangerous, Mayon brings good things too. Its ash makes the soil rich, so farmers around it can grow crops like rice and abaca.

questions.prompt: In what province is Mayon Volcano found?
The name Mayon comes from the Bikol word "magayon." What does magayon mean?
What is left of the town of Cagsawa today?
options: The bell tower of its old church

questions.prompt: Why do scientists watch Mayon closely?
options: So they can warn nearby people before it erupts
To measure how much it grows each day

passages.title: The Water Cycle
paragraphs: The water you drink today might once have been part of a cloud, an ocean, or even a dinosaur's drinking pond! That is because Earth keeps using the same water again and again in a never-ending journey called the water cycle.
The journey begins with evaporation. When the Sun heats water in oceans, rivers and lakes, some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. The vapor rises up into the sky.
High in the sky, the air is cooler. The water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny drops of water. This is called condensation. Millions of these tiny drops gather together to form clouds.
When the drops in a cloud join together and become too heavy, they fall back to the ground as rain, snow or hail. This step is called precipitation.
Finally, the water collects in oceans, lakes, rivers and under the ground. Plants and animals use some of it. Then the Sun warms the water again, and the cycle starts all over.

questions.prompt: Which step of the water cycle comes FIRST in the text?
What do we call it when water falls from clouds as rain, snow or hail?
What are clouds made of?
options: Millions of tiny drops of water

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Earth's water moves around in a cycle again and again

passages.title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
paragraphs: Once upon a time, a poor farmer and his wife lived in a small house with a few animals. One morning, the farmer went to collect eggs and found something amazing. In his goose's nest was an egg made of shining gold!

He could hardly believe it. He took the egg to the market and sold it for a lot of money. The next morning, the goose laid another golden egg, and the next morning, another. Soon the farmer and his wife were rich.
But as they grew richer, they also grew greedy. "One egg a day is too slow," said the farmer. "The goose must be full of gold inside. If we cut it open, we can take all the gold at once!"
So they did. But inside the goose they found no gold at all. It was just like any other goose. Now their goose was gone, and there would never be another golden egg.
The farmer and his wife learned a hard lesson: people who want too much, too fast, can end up losing everything they have.

questions.prompt: What did the farmer find in the goose's nest?
How many golden eggs did the goose lay each day?

options: They cut the goose open to get all the gold

questions.prompt: What is the lesson of this fable?
options: Wanting too much, too fast, can make you lose everything

passages.title: The Banaue Rice Terraces
paragraphs: High in the mountains of Ifugao, in the northern Philippines, giant green steps climb up the steep slopes. These are the Banaue Rice Terraces: flat fields carved into the mountainsides so that rice can grow where the land is too steep for ordinary farms.

The terraces were built by hand by the Ifugao people, using simple tools. They shaped the soil and built walls of mud and stone to hold each step in place. Experts still discuss exactly how old the terraces are, but families have farmed them for hundreds of years.

Water is the secret of the terraces. Forests at the tops of the mountains catch rainwater. Farmers then guide the water down through channels and bamboo pipes, from one terrace to the next, so every step gets the water its rice plants need.

Because they are so beautiful and important, the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. Today, young Ifugao farmers and visitors are learning how to care for them so they last for many more years.

questions.prompt: Why were the terraces carved into the mountains?
options: So rice can grow where the land is too steep for ordinary farms

questions.prompt: Which people built the rice terraces by hand?

options: Farmers guide it down through channels and bamboo pipes

questions.prompt: Why is it important to protect the forests above the terraces?
options: They catch the rainwater the rice needs
They are good places to park

passages.title: The Magic of Magnets
paragraphs: Have you ever stuck a picture to the refrigerator with a magnet? A magnet is an object that can pull certain metals toward it without even touching them. This invisible pull is called magnetic force.
Magnets attract things made of iron, nickel and steel, like paper clips and nails. But they do not attract wood, plastic, paper or glass. They do not even pull on aluminum cans.

Every magnet has two ends, called poles: a north pole and a south pole. If you hold two magnets close together, opposite poles pull toward each other, but poles that are the same push each other away. Scientists say that opposites attract and likes repel.

Earth itself acts like a giant magnet. That is why a compass works. The compass needle is a tiny magnet, and it turns until it points north. For hundreds of years, sailors and explorers have used compasses to find their way across the oceans.

questions.prompt: Which of these would a magnet pull toward it?
What are the two ends of a magnet called?
questions.answerText: Poles: a north pole and a south pole

questions.prompt: What would happen if you pushed the north poles of two magnets together?
options: They would push each other away

questions.prompt: Why does a compass needle point north?
options: It is a tiny magnet, and Earth acts like a giant magnet
It is painted to point that way

passages.title: Juan Tamad and the Guava Tree
paragraphs: Juan was a boy who did not like to work. He was so lazy that everyone in the village called him Juan Tamad, which means Lazy Juan.

One sunny afternoon, Juan's mother asked him to go to the market. On the way, he passed a guava tree full of ripe, sweet fruit. Juan's mouth watered. But instead of climbing the tree or shaking a branch, he lay down right under it.
"Why should I climb?" he said to himself. "I will just open my mouth and wait. Sooner or later, a guava will fall right in." So Juan lay there with his mouth wide open, waiting and waiting.

Hours passed. Ants crawled over his feet and the sun began to set, but not a single guava fell. When Juan finally went home, it was too late for the market, and his mother had nothing to cook for dinner. Juan was hungry, and he had no guavas either.
Filipinos still tell this funny story to remind children that good things come to those who work for them, not to those who just wait.

questions.prompt: What does "Tamad" mean in Juan's name?

questions.prompt: What lesson does the story teach?
options: Good things come to those who work for them, not those who just wait
